The imaginative stagecraft, in tandem with the choreography, actually does spark the childlike, wide-eyed wonder that has made this fantasy world so alluring.
If you have ever read a HARRY POTTER book or seen one of the films, you owe it to yourself to experience this one-of-a-kind staged phenomenon at least once.
Harry Potter and the Cursed Child at the Orpheum Theatre is a solid night out.

And as entertaining as it still turned out to be, it's still a little puzzling how it won a Best Play Tony considering how wordy and frantic it could be, and how emotionally clumsy and repetitive the father-and-son reunion themes became.
Harry Potter and the Cursed Child will always be a great production to watch because it’s great theatre in its stagecraft and in its performances.
As a A.C. touring show when compared to a B.C. sit down show, I'd give this a MEH+.
"Harry Potter and the Cursed Child" is an innovative marvel of the stage that must be seen to be believed.
To say it exceeded my expectations would be an understatement.
From the moment the show begins, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is FILLED with Hogwarts-level magic, bringing the wizarding world to life in a way that feels almost impossible.
Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is a fantastic show in both meanings of the word.
Hardcore Potterphiles should be very happy with the show, and even casual fans or people who have only seen the movies are sure to enjoy this truly magical production.

Nonetheless, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is a must-see for wizards, witches and muggles alike – an awe-inspiring, theatrical experience that proves the Wizarding World is just as magical on stage as it is on the page, and reminds us why the fascinating world of Harry Potter endures.
Tiffany seamlessly guides the spirited cast, keeping the pace steady and allowing the wondrous special effects to transform The Fox into a showcase for theatricality.
It’s a fully engrossing and even immersive experience.
It offers up so much theatrical magic that you won't be able to tear your eyes away from the stage.

“Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” offers a spellbinding saga, filled with incredible stage flair, otherworldly practical effects and, at times, unsettling pyrotechnics that will transport audience members into the wizarding world for a few hours.
The production includes some of the most astonishing theatrical immersive magic ever seen on stage.

The nearly three-hour show, now playing through Dec. 20 at the Emerson Colonial Theatre in Boston, triumphs with its dazzling on-stage spells, bringing the true magic of J.K. Rowling's world right to your eyes.
Twists, turns, rumors and revelations abound in this elaborate production tailor made for Harry Potter fans and for those who truly enjoy onstage wizardry!
It's a joyous, at times agreeably jumbled experience that was worth the wait.
If you’re going for awe, wonder, and one of the most technically impressive stage experiences to hit Minneapolis, this production casts a powerful spell.
The spectacle’s the thing here, and all those parts shine quite well individually.
Many talented theater professionals have put their all into this production, and it shows.
The show is enjoyable, fun and a decent companion to the series.

"Harry Potter and the Cursed Child," the Broadway touring production brought in by Zions Bank Broadway at the Eccles, offers magical live visual effects that seem to turn one character into another, spark fire battles with wizards' wands, and depict time travel between alternate realities.
But everything else? It's just pure magic.
Like I said, it is more a play to be enjoyed for the spectacle of it and the immersive experience rather than for the story or profundity of the message.
The result is a marvel of visual spectacle with an overly convoluted story which runs on too long for this revisit of Harry Potter, which became a pop culture phenomenon in the 1990s as author J.K.

Ultimately, however, despite a dreary series of 11th-hour scenes attempting to tug on audience’s heartstrings, the fundamental failure of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child ’s father-son story to connect emotionally makes all its stagecraft sorcery disappear in a puff of smoke.

Technically, the production is a marvel, a three-hour epic of time travel and magic. Those magic effects are amazing, amazing , often garnering gasps or full-voiced WOWs when characters disappear, reappear, fly through the air, swim through the air, get shot through the air, or transform into another character right before your eyes.

cn.t: Critics praise the spectacular stagecraft and visual effects, calling it a dazzling technical achievement that delights nostalgic fans, though some find the story convoluted and overly long.
